title: X-rays add new twist to narwhal's spiral tusk
gist: Synchrotron X-ray imaging of narwhal tusks reveals a hidden double-helix structure—a left-handed cementum spiral over a right-handed dentine spiral—that gives the tusk its strength and straightness, and may serve as an environmental record of the rapidly changing North Atlantic.

insights.claim: New synchrotron imaging shows the narwhal tusk has a second internal spiral: the cementum forms a left-handed helix while the dentine forms a right-handed one, and this double-helix gives the tusk its stiffness, strength, and ability to grow straight.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Biomimetic insight into strong, crack-resistant composite structures could inform materials science.

insights.claim: The study combined X-ray computed tomography, scanning X-ray diffraction, small-angle scattering, tensor tomography, and birefringence microscopy, requiring time on three large synchrotrons in Sweden, Switzerland, and France.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Illustrates the heavy instrumentation demand for atomic-to-macro structural biology.

insights.claim: Because whales can live up to 80 years, their teeth form a historical record of changing environmental conditions, which researchers now aim to use to trace rapid changes in the North Atlantic.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Positions the tusk as a potential climate archive—of scientific, not investor, interest.
insights.quote: their teeth form a kind of historical record of changing environmental conditions
